Paper_Info: Identifying Emotional States using Keystroke Dynamics | Clayton Epp, Michael Lippold, Regan L. Mandryk | NOT MENTIONED
Objective: Recognize emotional states using keystroke dynamics as a non-invasive, cost-effective method for emotionally-aware systems.
Methodology: Field study collecting keystroke data and self-reported emotional states. Keystroke features (key duration, latency) were extracted and used to train decision-tree classifiers for 15 emotional states.
Dataset: Keystroke data from participants performing daily tasks, labeled with self-reported emotional states via experience-sampling questionnaires.
Performance: Top results: 2-level classifiers for confidence (77.4%), hesitance (77.4%), nervousness (87.8%), relaxation (87.8%), sadness (87.8%), and tiredness (87.8%). Anger and excitement achieved 84% accuracy.
Limitations: Limited exploration of anger and excitement; reliance on self-reported emotional states may introduce bias.

Paper_Info: Behavioral Biometrics in Assisted Living: A Methodology for Emotion Recognition | Stefanos Xefteris, Nikos Doulamis, Vassiliki Andronikou, Theodora Varvarigou, George Cambourakis | 2016
Objective: Develop emotion recognition mechanisms for unobtrusive monitoring of neurodegenerative disease patients in smart healthcare environments.
Methodology: Combines computational geometry, image processing, graph theory for region detection, neural networks for classification, Paul Ekman's facial expression theory, and service-oriented architectures for real-time monitoring.
Performance: Achieved 85% fear recognition, 92% disgust, 97% joy, 67% anger, and 95% sadness accuracy. Integrated into ambient assisted living systems for remote cognitive/physical status estimation of MCI and dementia patients.
Limitations: Relies on specific biometric traits with dynamic variability; requires calibration for diverse populations and environmental conditions.

Paper_Info: Emotion Recognition through Keystroke Dynamics on Touchscreen Keyboards | Matthias Trojahn, Florian Arndt, Markus Weinmann, Frank Ortmeier | 2013
Objective: Improve human-computer interaction by automatically recognizing emotions through keystroke dynamics on touchscreen keyboards, addressing limitations of conventional keyboard methods.
Methodology: Developed an Android app and keyboard layout to record keystroke dynamics. Hypotheses derived from Yerkes-Dodson-Law and Flow theory. Conducted a study with 152 participants, analyzing data via SPSS to validate correlations between keystroke metrics and emotional states.
Dataset: Study involving 152 test persons with varying time limits (no time limit, 5 minutes, 3.5 minutes) and demographic data (age, gender, education).
Performance: Most hypotheses were confirmed: typing speed, error rate, and pressure correlate with emotional valence/arousal. Keystroke dynamics effectively explain and recognize emotional states under time pressure.
Limitations: Study limited to controlled lab environment and specific demographics (IT employees/students). Correlation does not imply causation in emotional responses.

Paper_Info: A Review of Emotion Recognition Methods Based on Keystroke Dynamics and Mouse Movements | A. Kołakowska | 2013
Methodology: Analyzing keystroke dynamics and mouse movements as biometric features, including data collection, feature extraction, and classifier training for emotion detection.
Dataset: Various studies with participants performing tasks (e.g., online shopping, typing exercises) to collect physiological and behavioral data under different emotional states.
Performance: Effectiveness of keystroke and mouse movement analysis in detecting emotional states, with challenges in data variability and labeling.
Limitations: Variability in data collection, lack of controlled emotional states, and limited sample sizes in some studies.

Paper_Info: Human Micro-Expression: A Novel Social Behavioral Biometric for Person Identification | ZAMAN WAHID, ASM HOSSAIN BARI, FAHIM ANZUM, MARINA L. GAVRILOVA | NOT MENTIONED
Objective: Introduce a novel Social Behavioral Biometric (SBB), human micro-expression, for person identification using behavioral patterns from social media.
Methodology: Emotion detection model extracts emotion probability scores from microblogs; emotion-progression features generated via dynamic time warping; rank-level weighted majority voting fusion improves identification accuracy.
Dataset: Proprietary benchmark dataset with 250 Twitter users' microblog samples.
Performance: High recognition rates on benchmark data; outperforms existing SBB traits in emotion-progression representation.
Limitations: Relies on statistical features; performance degrades with insufficient user data. Prior SBB traits limited by count-based feature generation.
